Virtual MCU - Datasheet


A 32-bit microcontroller modelled on the ARM Cortex-M3 (ARMv7-M architecture), on a board with LEDs, buttons, a buzzer, a UART, an I²C temperature sensor and an SPI shift register. This datasheet describes the CPU, the memory map, every register, the exception and interrupt system, the instruction set and the C compiler.



1. Overview




FeatureValue


CoreCortex-M3 style (ARMv7-M), Thumb-2 instruction subset, 32-bit; or Cortex-M33 style (ARMv8-M Mainline) with the DSP extension, a single-precision FPU, TrustZone, stack limit registers and the ARMv8-M MPU (chapter 11); or Cortex-M7 style (ARMv7E-M) with the DSP extension, a double-precision FPU, cache control registers and a 64 KB ITCM (chapter 12); or Cortex-A55 style (ARMv8.2-A, AArch64 assembly, EL0/EL1, Generic Timer, GIC: chapter 14). Two cores: chapter 13. Chosen with the Board list or #pragma core (User Manual 8.1)


Clock1 MHz virtual clock: 1 instruction = 1 cycle = 1 µs; exception entry adds 12 cycles


Code memoryat 0x08000000, 4 bytes per instruction (programs run as parsed instructions, not as binary machine code)


RAM64 KB at 0x20000000, little-endian


StacksMSP (main) and PSP (process), full-descending


ExceptionsReset, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick, one device interrupt line with 7 sources


PeripheralsGPIO (8 pins), UART, general-purpose timer, I²C master, SPI master, interrupt controller, 12-bit ADC (3 channels), hardware watchdog with reset cause, SysTick, SCB ICSR


On the board4 LEDs with selectable resistors, 2 push buttons, buzzer, potentiometer on the ADC, WDT light, I²C EEPROM (256 bytes at 0x50), USB-UART terminal, I²C temperature sensor at 0x48, 8-bit SPI shift register with LEDs






2. Core registers




RegisterDescription


r0-r12General-purpose registers. r0-r3 and r12 are saved automatically on exception entry.


sp (r13)Stack pointer. In thread mode it is MSP or PSP, chosen by CONTROL bit 1; in handler mode it is always MSP. Writes to sp keep the value as written.


lr (r14)Link register: the return address after BL/BLX, or an EXC_RETURN value inside a handler.


pc (r15)Program counter: the address of the current instruction (0x08000000 + 4 × index). The Registers window shows this address.


xPSRProgram status. Bits 31-28: flags N (negative), Z (zero), C (carry), V (overflow). Bit 24: T (Thumb), always 1. Bit 27: Q, the sticky saturation flag (set by SSAT/USAT and, on the Cortex-M33, by the saturating DSP instructions; MSR APSR_nzcvq, rN clears it). Bits 19-16: GE[3:0], set by the Cortex-M33's SIMD instructions. Bits 8-0: IPSR, the number of the active exception (0 in thread mode). Read it with MRS rN, APSR or IPSR.


MSPMain stack pointer. Set to the top of RAM (0x20010000) at reset. Used by handlers.


PSPProcess stack pointer. 0 at reset. Used by thread mode when CONTROL bit 1 is set (the VxWorks kernel runs tasks on PSP).


MSPLIM, PSPLIMCortex-M33 only: the stack limits of MSP and PSP (bits 2-0 read 0). 0 at reset (no limit). See 11.3.


PRIMASKBit 0 = 1 masks all interrupts (SVC is still taken). 1 at reset: interrupts start disabled. CPSIE i clears it, CPSID i sets it; or use MSR PRIMASK, rN.


CONTROLBit 1 (SPSEL): 0 = thread mode uses MSP, 1 = thread mode uses PSP. Bit 0 (nPRIV): 1 = thread mode is unprivileged (see 5.11); handlers always run privileged. Unprivileged code can read CONTROL but not write it. Bit 2 (FPCA) is 1 while a floating-point context is active, on the Cortex-M33 only (11.5); it reads 0 on the Cortex-M3.




Modes. The CPU is in thread mode when running normal code and in handler mode while an exception handler runs (IPSR not 0). The ISR light in the Registers window shows handler mode and which handler it is.



3. Memory map




RegionAddress rangeNotes


Code0x08000000 -Instruction i is at 0x08000000 + 4 × i. In linker-file builds, flash also holds data after the code (.rodata and the start values of .data), readable with LDR (10). Read-only. Data words written with .word (the vector table at the start) take one 4-byte slot each and read with LDR; instructions read as 0, as they are not stored as machine code. LDR rN, =label gives a code address.


RAM0x20000000 - 0x2000FFFF64 KB. C programs put global variables from the bottom up; the top 4 KB are kept for the main stack. VxWorks builds put the device tree blob just below that (9). Byte, half-word and word access at any alignment.


GPIO0x40010000 - 0x40010FFF32-bit registers. Use LDR / STR. Reading or writing an address that is not a register is a bus fault.


UART0x40011000 - 0x40011FFF


Timer (TIM)0x40012000 - 0x40012FFF


I²C0x40013000 - 0x40013FFF


SPI0x40014000 - 0x40014FFF


Interrupt controller (NVIC)0x40015000 - 0x40015FFF


ADC0x40016000 - 0x40016FFF


Watchdog (WDT)0x40017000 - 0x40017FFF


SysTick0xE000E010 - 0xE000E01CAt the standard Cortex-M address.


SCB CPUID0xE000ED00At the standard Cortex-M address; read only.


SCB ICSR0xE000ED04At the standard Cortex-M address.




Any other address gives Bus fault: read 0x… or write 0x…. The CPU stops, or starts HardFault_Handler if the program has one (HardFault).


Names. In assembly, GPIO UART TIM I2C SPI NVIC ADC WDT SYSTICK SCB RAM RAM_END are constants holding base addresses (LDR r4, =UART; SCB is 0xE000ED00, so ICSR is at SCB + 4). In C, every register is a variable named PERIPHERAL_REGISTER, for example UART_TX.



4. Reset and start-up


At reset (Build or Reset): RAM is cleared to 0; r0-r12 and lr are 0 (in VxWorks builds the device tree is then copied to RAM and r2 holds its address, see 9. Device tree); MSP = sp = 0x20010000 (RAM_END); PSP = 0; CONTROL = 0; PRIMASK = 1 (interrupts disabled); all peripheral registers are 0, and the watchdog is off. Execution starts at the label Reset_Handler, or at the first instruction. WDT_RSTCAUSE tells the program why it restarted: 1 = power-on (Build), 2 = the Reset button, 3 = the watchdog. A reset clears RAM but not the EEPROM; a watchdog reset also keeps the terminal text.


In a linker-file build (10) RAM is instead filled with 0xA5 at reset, as real RAM is not zero at power-on, and the program's own startup code (Reset_Handler) sets the stack, copies .data and zeroes .bss; no hidden start-up code is added.


For a C program the compiler adds start-up code: it initialises the global variables (__cinit), calls main(), and if main returns, loops at __halt. After a build or reset the debugger runs this start-up code and stops at the first line of your source. A program with its own Reset_Handler that does not use a linker file must call __cinit itself. All the examples, and every VxWorks program, use a linker file instead, so their startup.s sets up RAM itself.



5. Peripheral registers


All registers are 32 bits wide; unused bits read 0. Access: R = read, W = write, RW = both.



5.1 GPIO (base 0x40010000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0GPIO_DIRRWBits 7-0: direction of pins P7-P0. 1 = output, 0 = input.


0x4GPIO_OUTRWBits 7-0: the level driven on output pins.


0x8GPIO_INRBits 7-0: pin levels. An output pin reads its OUT bit; an input pin reads 1 while its button is pressed (P4, P5) and 0 otherwise.






PinConnected to


P0-P3LEDs D0 (red), D1 (green), D2 (amber), D3 (blue), each through a selectable resistor to ground


P4, P5Push buttons SW4, SW5 to 3V3 (pressed = 1); interrupt sources 2 and 3 when the pin is an input


P6Not connected


AIN0 (separate analog pin)Potentiometer, ADC channel 0


P7Buzzer BZ1




GPIO_DIR = 0x8F;                 /* LEDs and buzzer out, buttons in */
GPIO_OUT = GPIO_OUT | 0x01;      /* LED D0 on */
if (GPIO_IN & 0x10) { ... }      /* SW4 is pressed */



5.2 UART (base 0x40011000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0UART_TXWWriting sends bits 7-0 to the terminal. Transmission is instant.


0x4UART_STATUSRBit 0: TX ready (always 1). Bit 1: at least one received byte is waiting.


0x8UART_RXRReading returns the oldest received byte and removes it (0 if none is waiting). Bytes come from the Terminal input box.




Interrupt source 1 is pending while a received byte is waiting.



5.3 Timer (base 0x40012000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0TIM_COUNTRWFree-running counter of cycles (µs) since reset; it always counts, even when the timer is disabled. Writing sets the count.


0x4TIM_LOADRWPeriod in µs.


0x8TIM_CTRLRWBit 0: enable. Every write starts a new period of LOAD µs from now.


0xCTIM_FLAGRWReads 1 when the timer is enabled, LOAD > 0 and the period has elapsed. Any write clears it and starts the next period (one LOAD after the end of the previous one, so a periodic timer does not drift).




Interrupt source 0 is pending while FLAG reads 1, so a timer handler must write TIM_FLAG.


TIM_LOAD = 1000;                 /* 1 ms period */
TIM_CTRL = 1;                    /* start */
while (!TIM_FLAG) { }            /* wait 1 ms */
TIM_FLAG = 0;                    /* next period */



5.4 I²C master (base 0x40013000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0I2C_ADDRRWBits 6-0: 7-bit address of the device.


0x4I2C_DATARWBits 7-0: the byte to write, or the byte read.


0x8I2C_CTRLW1 = write DATA to the device. 2 = read a byte from the device into DATA. Add 4 (bit 2, STOP) to end the transfer after this byte; 4 alone just sends a STOP. Each byte completes at once.


0xCI2C_STATUSRBit 0: ACK, 1 if a device answered the last transfer.




Temperature sensor at 0x48. A write sets its register pointer to DATA. A read returns the register the pointer selects: register 0 is the temperature in °C (0-99, set with the slider on the board); other registers read 0. Without a device at the address, STATUS bit 0 is 0 (NACK) and a read gives 0xFF.


I2C_ADDR = 0x48;
I2C_DATA = 0;  I2C_CTRL = 1;     /* select register 0 */
I2C_CTRL = 2;                    /* read it */
if (I2C_STATUS & 1)
  temp = I2C_DATA;               /* degrees C */


Transfers. A transfer starts with the first byte after a STOP, after a change of I2C_ADDR, or with a write that follows a read (a repeated start). It ends with STOP. The temperature sensor treats every write as a new register pointer, so it works with or without STOP.


EEPROM at 0x50 (like a 24C02): 256 bytes, 0xFF when erased, kept across Reset, Build and page reloads (in your browser; Clear EEPROM on the board erases it).


    

  • Write: the first byte of a write transfer is the memory address; the following bytes are data, at most one 8-byte page (a write past the end of the page wraps to the start of the same page, as on real chips). The bytes are stored at the STOP; bytes never ended with a STOP are dropped when the next transfer starts.
    • 

  • Write cycle: after the STOP the chip stores the data for 5 ms and does not answer (NACK) meanwhile. Wait by sending its address until it answers ("acknowledge polling").
    • 

  • Read: write the memory address (no STOP), then read bytes; the address counts up after each byte, across pages. End the last read with STOP.
    • 



I2C_ADDR = 0x50;                                   /* store 0x12 0x34 at 16 */
I2C_DATA = 16;   I2C_CTRL = 1;                     /* memory address */
I2C_DATA = 0x12; I2C_CTRL = 1;
I2C_DATA = 0x34; I2C_CTRL = 1 | 4;                 /* last byte + STOP */
do { I2C_DATA = 0; I2C_CTRL = 1 | 4; } while (!(I2C_STATUS & 1));   /* wait 5 ms */
I2C_DATA = 16;   I2C_CTRL = 1;                     /* read it back */
I2C_CTRL = 2;     a = I2C_DATA;
I2C_CTRL = 2 | 4; b = I2C_DATA;



5.5 SPI master (base 0x40014000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0SPI_DATARWWriting sends bits 7-0 on MOSI to the 8-bit shift register, whose lights show the byte. At the same time a byte is received on MISO; reading SPI_DATA returns it.


0x4SPI_STATUSRBit 0: transfer done (always 1; transfers are instant).




The byte received is the next one from the board's MISO input box (the list repeats). The box takes hex digits two at a time: A5 3C, A53C and 0xA53C are the same two bytes and 12345 is 12 34 05. If the box is empty, the device returns the byte sent before (loopback).



5.6 Interrupt controller (base 0x40015000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0NVIC_ENRWEnable mask: bit n = 1 lets interrupt source n raise the device interrupt (bits 0-6 are used).


0x4NVIC_PENDRWRead: which sources are pending (enabled or not). Write 1 to bits 2-4 to clear those latched requests; bits 0, 1, 5 and 6 follow their source and are cleared at the source.


0x8NVIC_ACTIVERBit n = 1 while the handler of IRQ n is running or has been interrupted by a more urgent one.


0x10NVIC_PRI0RWPriorities of IRQ 0-3, one byte each: IRQ 0 in bits 7-0, IRQ 1 in 15-8, IRQ 2 in 23-16, IRQ 3 in 31-24. Byte writes work (*(volatile uint8_t *)0x40015012 = 0x40; sets IRQ 2).


0x14NVIC_PRI1RWPriorities of IRQ 4-6 (bits 7-0, 15-8, 23-16).




A priority byte is 0x00 (most urgent) to 0xF0 (least urgent): 4 bits are implemented, the upper half of the byte, so 16 levels in steps of 0x10 (the lower 4 bits read 0). All priorities are 0 after reset. See 6.3 for what they do and 6. Exceptions and interrupts for the sources.



5.7 SysTick timer (base 0xE000E010)




AddressC nameAccessDescription


0xE000E010SYST_CSRRWBit 0 ENABLE. Bit 1 TICKINT: raise the SysTick exception when the count reaches 0. Bit 2 CLKSOURCE: stored only; the timer always counts CPU cycles. Bit 16 COUNTFLAG: 1 if the count reached 0 since the last read; reading clears it. Enabling starts a period.


0xE000E014SYST_RVRRWReload value, bits 23-0. The period is RVR + 1 cycles (µs). RVR = 0 stops the timer.


0xE000E018SYST_CVRRWCurrent value, counting down. Any write clears COUNTFLAG and starts a new period.




SYST_RVR = 10000 - 1;            /* 10 ms period */
SYST_CVR = 0;
SYST_CSR = 7;                    /* enable, interrupt, CPU clock */



5.8 ADC (base 0x40016000)




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x0ADC_CTRLRWBits 1-0: channel. Writing with bit 4 set starts a conversion of that channel.


0x4ADC_STATUSRBit 0: done (a result is waiting). Bit 1: busy.


0x8ADC_DATARThe 12-bit result, 0-4095 for 0-3.3 V. Reading it clears "done".






ChannelInputValue


0Potentiometer on the board (pin AIN0)0-3.3 V as you drag it: 0-4095


1Internal temperature sensor0.5 V + 10 mV per °C (the board's temperature slider): 25 °C = 0.75 V = 931


2Internal reference1.2 V = 1489, to check readings


3Not connected0




A conversion takes 10 µs; the value is taken at its end. Interrupt source 5 is pending while "done" is set, so a handler reads ADC_DATA. Result to millivolts: mV = raw * 3300 / 4095.


ADC_CTRL = 0 | 0x10;             /* channel 0, start */
while (!(ADC_STATUS & 1)) { }    /* about 10 us */
raw = ADC_DATA;                  /* 0-4095 */



5.9 Watchdog (base 0x40017000)


The watchdog resets the CPU when a program stops working: once started, the program must kick it before the timeout, or the whole CPU is reset. It is off after every reset, so only a program that starts it is affected.




OffsetC nameAccessDescription


0x00WDT_CTRLRWBit 0: enable. Bit 1: early-warning interrupt. Bit 2: lock. A write counts only with the key 0x5A in bits 31-24 (for example 0x5A000001); other writes are ignored, so a stray write cannot start or stop it. Starting it starts a full timeout. Once locked, it cannot be stopped or unlocked until the next reset.


0x04WDT_RELOADRWTimeout in µs, 1 to 16,777,215 (about 16.7 s); 1,000,000 after reset. Used at the next start or kick.


0x08WDT_KICKWWrite 0xAAAA to start the timeout again. Other values do nothing.


0x0CWDT_COUNTRµs left before the reset (0 when off).


0x10WDT_STATUSRWBit 0: early warning (write 1 to clear). Bit 1: running.


0x14WDT_RSTCAUSERWhy the CPU last reset: 1 power-on (Build), 2 Reset button, 3 watchdog, 4 software reset (SCB_AIRCR).




    

  • Timeout: the CPU resets as at power-on (RAM cleared, watchdog off, the program starts again), the WDT light on the board flashes red, the status bar and Output say so, and WDT_RSTCAUSE reads 3. The EEPROM and the terminal text are kept. If it happens during a step, the step stops.
    • 

  • Early warning: with bit 1 set, interrupt source 6 becomes pending once, when a quarter of the timeout is left; the handler clears it by writing 1 to WDT_STATUS bit 0 (a kick clears it too).
    • 

  • Paused CPU: the watchdog counts virtual time, so it stops whenever the CPU is paused, at a breakpoint or between steps.
    • 

  • While it runs, the WDT light is green.
    • 



WDT_RELOAD = 500000;              /* 500 ms */
WDT_CTRL = 0x5A000001;            /* key + enable */
while (1) {
  work();
  WDT_KICK = 0xAAAA;              /* "still alive" */
}



5.10 SCB: ICSR (0xE000ED04) and the system handler priorities




BitNameDescription


28PENDSVSETWrite 1 to make PendSV pending. Reads 1 while it is pending.


27PENDSVCLRWrite 1 to remove a pending PendSV.


26PENDSTSETWrite 1 to make SysTick pending. Reads 1 while it is pending.


25PENDSTCLRWrite 1 to remove a pending SysTick.


8-0VECTACTIVERead: the active exception number (same as IPSR).




C name: SCB_ICSR. Operating systems use PendSV for the context switch: they set PENDSVSET, and the switch happens when no other handler is running.




AddressC nameDescription


0xE000ED00SCB_CPUIDRead only: which core this is. Reads 0x412FC231 on the Cortex-M3: implementer 0x41 (Arm, bits 31-24), variant 2 (bits 23-20), 0xF (bits 19-16), part number 0xC23 (bits 15-4), revision 1 (bits 3-0), the value of a Cortex-M3 r2p1. The emulator does not model the differences between revisions. A write is a bus fault.


0xE000ED0CSCB_AIRCRReads 0xFA050000. Bits 10-8 are PRIGROUP, the priority grouping (see section 6.3). Write the key 0x05FA in bits 31-16 together with the new PRIGROUP; add bit 2 (SYSRESETREQ, so 0x05FA0004) to reset the CPU as the Reset button does: WDT_RSTCAUSE becomes 4. A write with another key does nothing.


0xE000ED28SCB_CFSRWhy the last fault happened (write 1 to clear a bit). Bit 8: instruction bus error (a branch to an invalid address). Bit 9: data bus error (a read or write at an address with nothing there). Bit 15: SCB_BFAR holds the address. Bit 16: undefined instruction (the CPU ran into data).


0xE000ED2CSCB_HFSRBit 30 FORCED: the fault became a HardFault (always the case here; write 1 to clear).


0xE000ED34SCB_MMFARThe address of the access the MPU refused, valid when CFSR bit 7 (MMARVALID) is set.


0xE000ED38SCB_BFARThe address of the failed read or write, valid when CFSR bit 15 is set.


0xE000ED14SCB_CCRBit 4 DIV_0_TRP: a division by zero is a UsageFault. Bit 3 UNALIGN_TRP: an unaligned word or halfword access is a UsageFault. Bit 9 (stack alignment) always reads 1. Reads 0x200 after reset.


0xE000ED18SCB_SHPR1Bits 23-16: priority of UsageFault (6); bits 15-8: BusFault (5); bits 7-0: MemManage (4)


0xE000ED24SCB_SHCSRBits 18, 17, 16: UsageFault, BusFault, MemManage handler enabled (0 after reset, then a fault is a HardFault). Bits 0, 1, 3, 7, 10, 11 read 1 while MemManage, BusFault, UsageFault, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick are active.


0xE000ED1CSCB_SHPR2Bits 31-24: priority of SVCall (exception 11)


0xE000ED20SCB_SHPR3Bits 31-24: priority of SysTick (15); bits 23-16: priority of PendSV (14)




The same priority bytes as the NVIC's (0x00 most urgent ... 0xF0 least urgent; byte writes work). Operating systems usually give PendSV the least urgent priority, 0xF0, so that a context switch never interrupts an interrupt handler.



5.11 Memory protection unit (MPU) and unprivileged mode


The MPU of the Cortex-M3 follows the ARMv7-M one (PMSAv7): 8 regions (the Cortex-M33 has the ARMv8-M MPU instead: 11.4). It is off after reset. These registers are in the system region, so only privileged code reaches them:




AddressC nameDescription


0xE000ED90MPU_TYPEReads 0x00000800: 8 data regions, no separate instruction regions.


0xE000ED94MPU_CTRLBit 0 ENABLE. Bit 1 HFNMIENA: keep the MPU on inside NMI and HardFault handlers (off: they run unchecked). Bit 2 PRIVDEFENA: privileged code may use the normal memory map where no region matches.


0xE000ED98MPU_RNRThe region (0-7) that RBAR and RASR work on.


0xE000ED9CMPU_RBARBits 31-5: base address (the size of the region must divide it; the low bits are dropped). Write with bit 4 (VALID) set and the region in bits 3-0: RNR takes that number and the write goes to that region. Reads give the base and RNR.


0xE000EDA0MPU_RASRBit 0 ENABLE. Bits 5-1 SIZE: the region has 2SIZE+1 bytes (SIZE 4 = 32 bytes ... 31 = 4 GB). Bits 15-8 SRD: disable the sub-region (an eighth of the region) for each bit set (regions of 256 bytes or more). Bits 26-24 AP. Bit 28 XN (no instruction fetch). Bits 21-16 (TEX, S, C, B) are stored and have no effect here.


0xE000EDA4 … 0xE000EDB8RBAR_A1, RASR_A1 ... RASR_A3The same registers for the regions (RNR & ~3) + 1, + 2 and + 3 (several regions with one block write).






APPrivileged codeUnprivileged code


0no accessno access
1read, writeno access
2read, writeread
3read, writeread, write


4(reserved: no access)no access
5readno access
6, 7readread




What happens. With ENABLE set, every read, write and instruction fetch is checked. The enabled region with the highest number that contains the address decides (a disabled sub-region does not count); an instruction fetch also needs XN = 0 and read permission. If no region matches, privileged code is allowed when PRIVDEFENA is set, and everything else is refused. A refused access does not happen: the CPU raises a MemManage fault (exception 4) if SCB_SHCSR bit 16 is set and its priority allows (HardFault: otherwise a HardFault with FORCED). SCB_CFSR bit 1 (DACCVIOL, with bit 7 MMARVALID and the address in SCB_MMFAR) says a read or write was refused, bit 0 (IACCVIOL) an instruction fetch; the stacked pc is the instruction. The system region (0xE0000000 and up: SCB, NVIC, SysTick, the MPU itself) is never checked by the MPU. This emulator's choices: an access is checked at its first byte only; the pushes and pops of an exception are checked like other accesses but a refusal there stops the CPU with a message instead of raising MSTKERR or MUNSTKERR; the debugger's own memory writes are not checked; the memory attributes (TEX, S, C, B) have no effect.


Unprivileged mode. CONTROL bit 0 (nPRIV), set with MSR CONTROL or __set_CONTROL(1), makes thread mode unprivileged. Unprivileged code is checked against the AP column above; it cannot read or write the system region (NVIC, SysTick, SCB, MPU: a bus error, a HardFault unless the BusFault handler is on); MSR to the special registers and CPSID/CPSIE are ignored, MRS of PRIMASK, BASEPRI, MSP and PSP gives 0, and CONTROL can be read but not written. Exception handlers always run privileged, so the way back is an exception: an SVC whose handler clears nPRIV (__set_CONTROL(__get_CONTROL() & ~1)); CONTROL keeps its value when the exception returns. The Registers window shows nPRIV and the Peripherals window the MPU registers and the enabled regions in words. Not in this emulator: the MPU is not used by the VxWorks kernel (no stack guards, no protected tasks), and there is no FAULTMASK.


Stacking errors. When an exception is taken, the CPU pushes eight words (the frame) on the current stack. If the MPU refuses one of those writes (a stack that ran into a no-access region), the frame is not written, CFSR bit 4 (MSTKERR) is set and the MemManage handler runs instead of the exception, on the main stack, so it can still work; with no MemManage handler (SHCSR bit 16 off) the CPU stops as before. The faulted frame cannot be returned to. This emulator's own simplification: on a real chip the original exception is entered as well; MMFAR is not set for a stacking error. The VxWorks kernel uses this for its task stack guards.


The example samples/mpu.c protects 256 bytes of RAM so that unprivileged code may read but not write them: the unprivileged write is refused and skipped by the MemManage handler, and an SVC gives privilege back. With the Cortex-M33 chosen the same file programs the ARMv8-M MPU (Datasheet chapter 11): there is no "unprivileged read-only, privileged read/write" setting, so the protected words are read-only for everybody until the program makes them writable after the SVC.





6. Exceptions and interrupts


6.1 The vector table


As on a real Cortex-M3, the CPU finds its handlers in a vector table at 0x08000000: one 4-byte word per entry. At reset it loads word 0 into SP and starts at the address in word 1. When exception n is taken, it starts at the address in word n. The table is the .isr_vector section of every example's startup.s, written with .word; the linker file puts it first in FLASH (KEEP(*(.isr_vector))), and the code follows at 0x0800005C. Look at it in the Memory window at 0x08000000, or at the top of the Disassembly window.




Number (IPSR)AddressEntryName in startup.sCaused by


00x08000000Initial stack pointer_estackloaded into SP at reset


10x08000004ResetReset_HandlerBuild, Reset, a watchdog reset


2-60x08000008-18NMI, HardFault, MemManage, BusFault, UsageFaultNMI_Handler … UsageFault_HandlerHardFault (3), BusFault (5) and UsageFault (6) are raised by faults (see HardFault below); MemManage (4) is raised when the memory protection unit refuses an access (see 5.11)


110x0800002CSVCallSVC_Handlerthe SVC #n instruction


140x08000038PendSVPendSV_Handlerwriting ICSR bit 28


150x0800003CSysTickSysTick_HandlerSysTick reaching 0 with TICKINT set, or ICSR bit 26


160x08000040IRQ 0: timerTIM_IRQHandlertimer period elapsed


170x08000044IRQ 1: UARTUART_IRQHandlera byte has arrived


180x08000048IRQ 2: SW4SW4_IRQHandlerSW4 pressed


190x0800004CIRQ 3: SW5SW5_IRQHandlerSW5 pressed


200x08000050IRQ 4(0, not used)


210x08000054IRQ 5: ADCADC_IRQHandlerconversion done


220x08000058IRQ 6: watchdogWDT_IRQHandlerearly warning


230x0800005CIRQ 7: messaging unitMU_IRQHandlertwo-core programs only (13.1); the samples' tables stop at 22




Every handler name is weak (.weak NAME and .thumb_set NAME, Default_Handler): when the program defines a function with that name, the table holds its address; otherwise the name means Default_Handler, a loop where the CPU then waits (in the debugger, IPSR tells which exception it was). An entry of 0 for an exception that happens, an address that is not code, or an entry the table does not have, stops the CPU with a fault naming the entry.


Programs without a vector table (assembly files such as interrupts.s, and C files without startup code) work by name instead: Reset_Handler, SVC_Handler, PendSV_Handler, SysTick_Handler, and one handler for all device interrupts, IRQ_Handler (or the label named by .vector label), which reads NVIC_PEND to see which sources are pending. They then share exception 16.



6.2 Device interrupt sources




Bit in NVIC_EN / NVIC_PENDSourceKindHow the handler clears it


0Timer period elapsedlevel (while TIM_FLAG reads 1)write TIM_FLAG


1UART byte receivedlevel (while bytes are waiting)read UART_RX until empty


2SW4 pressed, P4 an inputlatched on the presswrite 4 to NVIC_PEND


3SW5 pressed, P5 an inputlatched on the presswrite 8 to NVIC_PEND


4Without a vector table: SVC executed when there is no SVC_Handler. Not used with a table.latchedwrite 16 to NVIC_PEND


5ADC conversion donelevel (while done)read ADC_DATA


6Watchdog early warninglevel (until cleared)write 1 to WDT_STATUS, or kick




With a vector table, source n is IRQ n: exception 16 + n, with its own handler. Without one, all sources share exception 16 and IRQ_Handler reads NVIC_PEND. Either way, a source that is still pending when its handler returns enters the handler again at once.



6.3 Priorities and nesting


With a vector table, every exception has a priority: SVCall, PendSV and SysTick in SCB_SHPR2/SCB_SHPR3 (5.10), IRQ n in NVIC_PRI0/NVIC_PRI1 (5.6). A smaller number is more urgent. The CPU runs at an execution priority: that of the most urgent active handler (in thread mode, none), lowered further by BASEPRI.


    

  • A pending exception is taken when its priority is more urgent (smaller) than the execution priority. If a handler is running, it is interrupted: the new handler nests on top of it, and the interrupted one continues when the new one returns (lr holds 0xFFFFFFF1 in the nested handler).
    • 

  • An exception with the same or a less urgent priority waits until the running handler returns.
    • 

  • When several are pending, the most urgent goes first; at equal priority, the lowest exception number (PendSV 14, SysTick 15, then IRQ 0, 1, …). With priority grouping (next point) the order is group priority, then sub-priority, then exception number.
    • 

  • Priority grouping. Bits 10-8 of SCB_AIRCR (PRIGROUP, written with the key 0x05FA in bits 31-16, 0 after reset) split each priority byte into a group priority (the upper bits) and a sub-priority (the lower bits). Only the group priority decides pre-emption: an exception pre-empts a running handler only if its group priority is more urgent. The sub-priority only orders exceptions that are pending at the same time and have the same group priority. PRIGROUP g makes bits 7 down to g+1 the group and bits g down to 0 the sub-priority. With the 4 implemented bits (7-4), PRIGROUP 0 to 3 are all the same (all four bits are group priority, no sub-priority); 4 gives 3 group bits and 1 sub-priority bit; 5 gives 2 and 2; 6 gives 1 and 3; 7 gives 0 and 4 (no exception pre-empts another). This emulator's own choice, not verified against the ARM manual: BASEPRI also compares the group priority only.
    • 

  • PRIMASK (__disable_irq(), CPSID i) blocks every exception except SVC. BASEPRI (MSR BASEPRI, rN, __set_BASEPRI(x)) blocks only exceptions with priority x or less urgent; 0 turns it off.
    • 

  • SVC is taken immediately when the instruction executes, even when interrupts are disabled and inside a handler.
    • 

  • All priorities are 0 after reset, so by default nothing nests: the program sets priorities to allow it. The VxWorks kernel leaves them all equal.
    • 

  • WFI and WFE wait (one cycle at a time) until an exception is pending.
    • 

  • With a vector table, an exception without a handler of its own runs Default_Handler; an entry of 0 stops the CPU with a fault. A fault (a bad address, a bad branch, running into data) starts HardFault_Handler if the program defines it; otherwise it stops the CPU with the message (see HardFault below).
    • 



Without a vector table there are no priorities: one handler at a time, device interrupt first, then SysTick, then PendSV.


The example samples/priority.c shows nesting: a slow timer handler at a low priority, interrupted by SW4 at a high one; SW5, at the timer's priority, waits.




HardFault. These faults start HardFault_Handler (exception 3, entry 3 of the vector table): a read or write at an address with nothing there (a bus fault), a branch to an address that is not code, and running into data. The CPU pushes r0-r3, r12, lr, the pc and xPSR as for any exception; the stacked pc is the instruction that failed (the word at offset 24 of the frame), so a handler that adds 4 to it and returns skips that instruction. HardFault has priority -1: no interrupt can interrupt it. SCB_CFSR, SCB_HFSR and SCB_BFAR say what happened. As on a real chip after reset, the separate BusFault, UsageFault and MemManage handlers are off, so every fault is a HardFault with FORCED set until the program switches them on (next paragraph). A fault inside HardFault_Handler is a lockup: the CPU stops with the message Lockup: …. If the program has no HardFault_Handler (the table holds Default_Handler), the CPU stops with the message as before, and the status registers are set anyway. Programs without a vector table always stop. The usual last step of a handler is to reset the CPU with SCB_AIRCR = 0x05FA0004. This emulator's own choices: the stacked pc of a bad branch is the branch instruction (a real CPU stacks the bad target); a fault in the middle of a multi-register instruction (PUSH, POP, LDM, STM) is not precise.


BusFault, UsageFault and MemManage. Three bits of SCB_SHCSR switch on the separate handlers: bit 17 BusFault_Handler (exception 5), bit 18 UsageFault_Handler (exception 6), bit 16 MemManage_Handler (exception 4). All are off after reset. SCB_SHPR1 sets their priorities (byte 0 MemManage, 1 BusFault, 2 UsageFault; 0x00 most urgent, 0xF0 least). A bus fault (a bad read or write, a branch to an address that is not code) goes to BusFault_Handler, with SCB_CFSR bit 9 (data) or bit 8 (branch) and, for data, bit 15 and SCB_BFAR. Running into data is an undefined instruction (CFSR bit 16) and goes to UsageFault_Handler. Two bits of SCB_CCR add more UsageFaults: bit 4 DIV_0_TRP (a division by zero, CFSR bit 25; without the bit it gives 0) and bit 3 UNALIGN_TRP (an unaligned word or halfword load or store, CFSR bit 24; without the bit it works). The handler runs only if its priority is more urgent than what is running now; otherwise, or if its switch is off, the fault becomes a HardFault with HFSR bit 30 (FORCED) set, as does a fault inside one of these handlers. HFSR stays 0 when the specific handler ran. An enabled handler that the program does not define waits in Default_Handler (IPSR 5 or 6). SCB_SHCSR bits 0, 1, 3, 7, 10 and 11 read 1 while MemManage, BusFault, UsageFault, SVCall, PendSV or SysTick are active. MemManage is raised by the memory protection unit (5.11): CFSR bit 1 (DACCVIOL, a refused read or write, with MMARVALID bit 7 and SCB_MMFAR holding the address) or bit 0 (IACCVIOL, a refused instruction fetch). Unaligned LDM, STM and LDRD, and the other UsageFault causes of a real chip (coprocessor, invalid state), do not exist here. This emulator's own choice: SCB_CCR bit 9 (stack alignment) always reads 1.


The example samples/faults.c switches on both handlers (faults.s finds the stacked registers), then causes a bad write (BusFault), a division by zero (UsageFault) and, with BusFault switched off again, the same bad write: it escalates to HardFault.




The example samples/hardfault.c writes to an address that does not exist. Its handler (hardfault.s finds the stacked registers, then a C function prints them) shows the pc, CFSR, HFSR and BFAR and resets the CPU; the program starts again and reports reset cause 4.





6.4 Entry and return


On entry, as on a Cortex-M3, the CPU:


    

  1. pushes 8 words on the stack in use (PSP if thread mode uses it, else MSP), first aligning the stack to 8 bytes (if a padding word is added, bit 9 of the stacked xPSR is set);
    2. 

  2. switches to handler mode, which always uses MSP, and sets IPSR to the exception number;
    3. 

  3. puts an EXC_RETURN value in lr and jumps to the handler. This takes 12 cycles.
    4. 





Stack offset+0+4+8+12+16+20+24+28


Saved valuer0r1r2r3r12lrreturn addressxPSR






EXC_RETURN in lrMeaning


0xFFFFFFF1return to the interrupted handler (handler mode, MSP): in a nested handler


0xFFFFFFF9return to thread mode, using MSP


0xFFFFFFFDreturn to thread mode, using PSP




The handler returns with BX lr, POP {…, pc} or LDM …{…, pc} loading the EXC_RETURN value: the CPU pops the 8 words, restores the flags and continues the interrupted code. A handler written in C is an ordinary function with the handler's name; the compiler's function entry and exit save r4-r11 and return through lr, so no special keyword is needed.



6.5 Example: timer and button interrupts in C


This example has no startup code, so it uses the single IRQ_Handler. With a vector table (every example, and any program with #pragma link "startup.s"), write one function per interrupt instead: void TIM_IRQHandler(void), void SW4_IRQHandler(void); see samples/interrupts.c.


/* irqdemo/main.c - timer interrupt every 100 ms, SW4 interrupt on a press */
int ticks;

void IRQ_Handler(void)
{
  if (NVIC_PEND & 1) {           /* source 0: timer */
    TIM_FLAG = 0;                /* clear it, or the handler runs again */
    ticks++;
    GPIO_OUT = GPIO_OUT ^ 1;
    uart_puts("tick\n");
  }
  if (NVIC_PEND & 4) {           /* source 2: SW4 pressed */
    NVIC_PEND = 4;               /* clear the latched request */
    uart_puts("SW4\n");
  }
}

void main(void)
{
  GPIO_DIR = 0x01;               /* P0 out, P4 (SW4) in */
  TIM_LOAD = 100000;             /* 100 ms */
  TIM_CTRL = 1;
  NVIC_EN = 1 | 4;               /* enable sources 0 and 2 */
  __enable_irq();
  while (1) {
    __wfi();                     /* sleep until an interrupt */
  }
}

GroupInstructions

Logic and shiftsAND ORR ORN EOR BIC LSL LSR ASR ROR RRX


CompareCMP CMN TST TEQ


Bit field and byteCLZ RBIT REV REV16 REVSH SXTB SXTH UXTB UXTH BFC BFI UBFX SBFX SSAT USAT


Load and storeLDR STR LDRB STRB LDRH STRH LDRSB LDRSH LDRD STRD LDREX STREX LDM STM (IA, DB, FD, optional !) PUSH POP


BranchB BL BX BLX (register) CBZ CBNZ; B with conditions EQ NE CS/HS CC/LO MI PL VS VC HI LS GE LT GT LE


SystemMRS MSR (MSP, PSP, PRIMASK, BASEPRI, CONTROL, IPSR, APSR, APSR_nzcvq) CPSIE CPSID WFI WFE SEV SVC DMB DSB ISB CLREX NOP BKPT


Cortex-M33 onlythe DSP extension, load-acquire / store-release, TT, MSPLIM/PSPLIM: 11.2. On the Cortex-M3 the assembler refuses them ("QADD is not an instruction of the Cortex-M3").




A trailing S (for example ADDS, SUBS) updates the flags. Operands: registers, immediates #n (decimal or 0x hex), LDR rN, =value or =label, addressing [rN], [rN, #imm] and [rN, rM]. BKPT pauses the CPU (the debugger shows where).


Directives: .equ name, value; .word value, … (data words in flash: numbers, .equ symbols, labels); .byte, .hword (also .short, .2byte), .ascii, .asciz (also .string) and .space N[, fill] (also .skip) for bytes, halfwords, text and blocks of bytes: the bytes of consecutive data lines are packed little-endian into 4-byte words and the last word is padded with zeros, and a label, a .word, .align or an instruction ends the run, so a label always points to the start of a word (read single bytes with LDRB rN, [rM, #i]); values are numbers, .equ symbols or characters such as 'A', and .byte/.hword reject values that do not fit; .section .isr_vector … .section .text (the vector table, placed first at 0x08000000); .weak NAME with .thumb_set NAME, LABEL (NAME means LABEL unless the program defines NAME); .vector label (the device interrupt handler of a program without a table); .org address (this emulator's own form: an absolute flash address; the gap before it is filled with words that fault when run; used for TrustZone programs); .include "file". .global .thumb .syntax .text .align .type and similar are accepted and ignored. Labels end with :.


Not implemented: IT blocks, shifted register operands (ADD r0, r1, r2, LSL #2), pre- and post-indexed addressing, TBB/TBH, ADR, labels inside a run of .byte/.hword data (a label points to a whole word), coprocessor and floating-point instructions.



8. C compiler


A .c file is compiled to assembly for this CPU; the Disassembly window shows the result next to the source.


8.1 Language




Supported


Typesint unsigned signed char short long, long long (64 bits), float and double (section 4.11), uint8_t … int64_t and uint64_t, intptr_t, ptrdiff_t, bool/_Bool, size_t, pointers (also to functions), arrays of any dimension, struct, union, enum, typedef. char is unsigned; char and short variables are stored in 1 and 2 bytes; short and signed char are sign-extended when read. Bit-fields, anonymous members, __attribute__((packed)). Struct fields are aligned to their size (a 4-byte field starts at a multiple of 4), so a struct can contain padding; sizeof includes it.


Variablesglobal, local, static local; initialisers {1, 2, 3}, "text", nested {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, designated {.x = 1} and {[2] = 5}; an array size can come from its initialiser (int a[] = {1, 2}); elements and fields left out are 0


Statementsif else while do for switch case default break continue return goto (with labels), __asm("nop"), _Static_assert; assignment, ++ and -- also inside expressions (a[i++] = c, while ((c = next()) != 0), x = y = 0), the comma in for (i = 0, j = 9; ...; i++, j--) and in parentheses; structs are copied with =, passed to functions, returned and made with compound literals


Operatorsarithmetic, bitwise, comparison, logical, ?:, casts, sizeof (of a type or an expression), offsetof, & and *, . and ->, [ ] on arrays, pointers and string literals, calls through any function pointer (ops[i](x), p->fn(x)); pointer arithmetic counts in elements (p + 1, q - p)


Functionsany number of arguments, recursion, function pointers (typedef int (*FUNCPTR)(...)), variadic functions with va_list va_start va_arg va_end


Preprocessor#include "file" and <file>, #define NAME value and function-like macros (#, ##, __VA_ARGS__), #undef, #if #ifdef #ifndef #elif #else #endif with defined(), #error, #pragma link "file", #pragma linker "file"


Built-in functionsdelay_us(n) uart_putc(c) uart_puts(s) (unless you define your own); __enable_irq() __disable_irq() __wfi() __wfe() __nop() __bkpt() __ISB() __DSB() __DMB(); __get_PRIMASK() __set_PRIMASK(x) __get_BASEPRI() __set_BASEPRI(x) __get_IPSR() __get_PSP() __set_PSP(x) __get_MSP() __set_MSP(x) __get_CONTROL() __set_CONTROL(x)


Register variables (bare metal only)ADC_CTRL ADC_STATUS ADC_DATA WDT_CTRL WDT_RELOAD WDT_KICK WDT_COUNT WDT_STATUS WDT_RSTCAUSE GPIO_DIR GPIO_OUT GPIO_IN UART_TX UART_STATUS UART_RX TIM_COUNT TIM_LOAD TIM_CTRL TIM_FLAG I2C_ADDR I2C_DATA I2C_CTRL I2C_STATUS SPI_DATA SPI_STATUS NVIC_EN NVIC_PEND NVIC_ACTIVE NVIC_PRI0 NVIC_PRI1 SYST_CSR SYST_RVR SYST_CVR SCB_CPUID SCB_ICSR SCB_AIRCR SCB_CCR SCB_SHPR1 SCB_SHCSR SCB_CFSR SCB_HFSR SCB_BFAR SCB_MMFAR SCB_SHPR2 SCB_SHPR3 MPU_TYPE MPU_CTRL MPU_RNR MPU_RBAR MPU_RASR




Not supported: maths library functions beyond those listed in section 4.11, a struct value at file scope outside an initialiser of the same type, switch on a 64-bit value, variable-length arrays, and inline assembly with operands. / % < > <= >= and >> follow the types: unsigned if an operand is unsigned (also a pointer, sizeof or a constant above 0x7FFFFFFF), signed otherwise, with >> arithmetic for signed values. Section 4.10 describes the C features beyond the basics.


8.2 Calling convention and stack frame


Like the ARM AAPCS: arguments 1-4 in r0-r3, further arguments on the stack, the result in r0. (A struct passed by value, and a struct result, follow this emulator's own rules: section 4.10. A long long or double takes two words, low word first, which may be split between r3 and the stack, and comes back in r0:r1; a float travels as its 32 bits like an int and floating-point operations call the soft-float routines of section 4.11 (on the Cortex-M33, float operations use the FPU: 11.5): this is not the ARM hard-float convention, and not AAPCS for 64-bit values.) A function keeps r4-r11 unchanged for its caller. r11 is the frame pointer. Every function starts with


PUSH {r4-r11, lr}      @ save the caller's registers and the return address
MOV  r11, sp           @ frame pointer
SUB  sp, sp, #n        @ room for the local variables


so locals are at [r11, #-k], the saved r11 of the caller at [r11, #28], the return address at [r11, #32] and stack arguments from [r11, #36]. The debugger follows this chain for the Call stack. Expressions use r4-r9 for intermediate values (hence the limit of six) and r10, r12 as scratch registers. Global variables are available to assembly files by name.



9. Device tree (VxWorks builds)


A device tree describes the hardware of a board as data, so that an operating system can find its devices without fixed addresses in its code. Virtual ARM Lab uses one for VxWorks programs only; bare-metal programs have none.


9.1 How it reaches the CPU


    

  1. vxWorks.h contains #pragma devicetree "board.dts". When Build sees it, it compiles vxworks/board.dts to a flattened device tree blob (DTB): the standard binary format, version 17, big-endian, with a header, an empty memory reservation list, the structure block and the strings block.
    2. 

  2. At reset the DTB is copied to RAM just below the 4 KB reserved for the main stack (the Output window shows the address, 0x2000E7B0 for the board file as shipped), and r2 holds its address, the way an ARM boot loader hands a device tree to a kernel. The C compiler keeps global variables below the DTB.
    3. 

  3. startup.s keeps r2 and passes it to usrInit(dtb), which calls sysHwInit(dtb) before anything else.
    4. 



You can look at the blob in the Memory window: it starts with the magic number D0 0D FE ED.


9.2 Source syntax


The compiler accepts this subset of the device tree source format:




FormExample


Version line (required, first)/dts-v1/;


Root node; several are merged/ { … };


Node with unit address, and a labeluart0: serial@40011000 { … };


Extend a labelled node&uart0 { status = "disabled"; };


Property without valueinterrupt-controller;


Strings, string listscompatible = "varm,uart";, compatible = "a", "b";


Cells (32-bit numbers, decimal or 0x hex), phandle referencesreg = <0x40011000 0xc>;, gpios = <&gpio 0 0>;


Bytesmac = [00 11 22 33];


Path reference (outside < >)stdout-path = &uart0; becomes "/soc/serial@40011000"


Comments// … and /* … */




A node referenced with &label inside < > gets a phandle property automatically. Not supported: /include/ and #include, /delete-node/, /memreserve/, /bits/, macros and expressions in cells. Errors give the file and line.


9.3 The board file




NodecompatibleMain properties


/chosenstdout-path: the console UART


/cpus/cpu@0arm,cortex-m3clock-frequency 1000000. The IDE reads compatible to choose the core (User Manual 8.1); this version has one cpu node; "arm,cortex-m33" builds the program for the Cortex-M33 (chapter 11), "arm,cortex-m7" for the Cortex-M7 (chapter 12); "arm,cortex-a55" is refused (VxWorks runs on the Cortex-M cores here)


/memory@20000000(device_type "memory")reg 0x20000000, 64 KB


/soc/interrupt-controller@40015000varm,intcreg; interrupt-controller; label intc, the root's interrupt-parent


/soc/timer@e000e010arm,armv7m-systickreg, clock-frequency: the system clock


/soc/gpio@40010000varm,gpioreg, ngpios 8, #gpio-cells 2


/soc/serial@40011000varm,uartreg, interrupts 1


/soc/timer@40012000varm,timerreg, interrupts 0, clock-frequency


/soc/i2c@40013000 and temp-sensor@48varm,i2c / varm,temp-sensorreg; the sensor's reg is its I²C address


/soc/spi@40014000 and shift-register@0varm,spi / varm,shift-registerreg


/leds with led0 … led3gpio-ledseach LED: gpios = <&gpio pin flags>, flags bit 0 = active low; label


/keys with sw4, sw5gpio-keyseach key: gpios, interrupts 2 / 3


/buzzergpio-beepergpios = <&gpio 7 0>


/soc/adc@40016000varm,adcreg, interrupts 5, varm,num-channels 3; label adc0

/soc/i2c@40013000/eeprom@50varm,eepromreg = its I²C address, size 256, pagesize 8; label eeprom




The varm, compatible strings are this emulator's own. The others are borrowed from common device tree bindings (as used by Linux; not checked against the binding documents), but the drivers here implement only what this board needs; real bindings have more rules. The SysTick timer and the SCB are part of the Cortex-M core: the SCB is at a fixed address and is not in the tree; SysTick is in it so its clock can be configured.



10. Linker file


A C program with #pragma linker "app.ld" is laid out by that linker file instead of by the compiler. The compiler then puts each global into a section, the linker file places the sections in memory, and the program's startup code prepares RAM before main(). Every example uses one; VxWorks programs use vxworks/vxWorks.ld, which also keeps room for the device tree blob (_Dtb_Size) below the main stack.


10.1 Sections




SectionHoldsPlaced (example app.ld)


.isr_vectorthe vector table from startup.s (6.1)FLASH at 0x08000000, first (KEEP(*(.isr_vector))): the CPU reads it there at reset


.textthe codeFLASH, directly after the vector table (at 0x08000000 when the program has none)


.rodatastring constantsFLASH, after the code


.dataglobals and statics with a start valueruns in RAM (> RAM); the start values are stored in FLASH (AT > FLASH) for the startup code to copy


.bss (and COMMON)globals and statics without a start value (they start at 0)RAM, after .data; the startup code zeroes it




Variables keep their source order within .data and .bss. A function's address in an initialiser is a relocation that the link step fills in. Locals stay on the stack, as before.


10.2 Linker file syntax


A subset of the GNU ld script language:




FormExample


Memory regionsMEMORY { FLASH (rx) : ORIGIN = 0x08000000, LENGTH = 256K  RAM (rwx) : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 64K }


Output section in a region.text : { *(.text) *(.text*) } > FLASH


Run address and load address.data : { … } > RAM AT > FLASH


Input sections*(.text) *(.rodata*) *(.data*) *(.bss*) *(COMMON) KEEP(…); others are accepted and stay empty


Symbols and the location counter_sdata = .; . = ALIGN(4); . = . + _Min_Stack_Size; PROVIDE(sym = expr);


FunctionsORIGIN(R) LENGTH(R) ADDR(.s) LOADADDR(.s) SIZEOF(.s) ALIGN(n)


Numbers and operators0x1000, 4096, 4K, 1M; + - * / % << >> & | ~ and parentheses


Also acceptedENTRY(Reset_Handler), OUTPUT_FORMAT(…), OUTPUT_ARCH(…), comments /* … */




A symbol may be used before the line that defines it (for example _sidata = LOADADDR(.data); written before .data). Not supported: INCLUDE, overlays, file name patterns other than *. Names may contain -, so write spaces around minus signs. Errors give the file and line; Build also checks that each section fits its region, that .data and .bss are in the board's 64 KB of RAM, and that .data has a load address in flash.


10.3 Symbols and startup code


Every symbol the linker file defines is available to assembly as a constant (LDR r0, =_sbss) and in the Watch window, where it shows as an address. The example uses the names common in Cortex-M startup files:




SymbolMeaning


_estackinitial stack pointer (top of RAM); the stack grows down from it


_sidataaddress in flash of the start values of .data (LOADADDR(.data))


_sdata, _edatastart and end of .data in RAM


_sbss, _ebssstart and end of .bss


_etextend of the code


_Min_Stack_Sizestack space that must stay free; reserved by the last section so that an overflow is a build error




The startup code (Reset_Handler, required) runs first. The CPU also starts with the stack pointer at the top of RAM, but the startup code sets it from _estack, so moving _estack in the linker file moves the stack. RAM starts filled with 0xA5, so a missing copy or zero loop shows up as wrong start values.


        LDR   r0, =_sbss        @ zero .bss
        LDR   r1, =_ebss
        MOV   r3, #0
zero_bss:
        CMP   r0, r1
        BCS   zero_done         @ done when r0 >= r1
        STR   r3, [r0]
        ADD   r0, r0, #4
        B     zero_bss
zero_done:


After Build, the Output window shows the memory map: each section with its address, size and region (and load address), the use of each region, and the symbols.



11. The Cortex-M33 core


Choose it with the Board list, #pragma core "cortex-m33", or compatible = "arm,cortex-m33" in the cpu@0 node of a VxWorks board.dts (User Manual 8.1). Everything in chapters 1-10 applies, with the additions below. Programs written for the Cortex-M3 build and run unchanged, except ones that program the ARMv7-M MPU registers directly (samples/mpu.c has an ARMv8-M branch under #ifdef __ARM_ARCH_8M_MAIN__). Try .


11.1 This emulator's Cortex-M33




ItemValue


ArchitectureARMv8-M Mainline, Thumb-2 with the DSP extension, the floating-point extension and the Security Extension (TrustZone)


SCB_CPUID0x410FD213 (Arm, part 0xD21, r0p3: the value QEMU's Cortex-M33 model uses)


MPUARMv8-M (PMSAv8), 8 regions


FPUFPv5 single precision (FPv5-SP-D16): S0-S31, FPSCR (11.5); MVFR0-2 read 0x10110021, 0x11000011, 0x00000040 (the values QEMU's M33 model reports)


TrustZonethe Security Extension: Secure and Non-secure states, SAU with 8 regions, no IDAU (11.6)


Not here The M33's own options (FPU, DSP, TrustZone, number of MPU regions) are chosen when a chip is designed; which ones NXP chose for the i.MX 93 was not checked, so this is this emulator's own configuration.


Timingas on the Cortex-M3: 1 instruction = 1 cycle (a real M33 takes 1 cycle for most DSP instructions too, but not for all; not modelled)




11.2 Instructions and C intrinsics




GroupInstructionsC (CMSIS names)


SaturatingQADD QSUB QDADD QDSUB (set Q), SSAT16 USAT16__QADD __QSUB __SSAT16(x, n) __USAT16(x, n); __SSAT(x, n) and __USAT(x, n) work on both cores


SIMD add/subtract (4 bytes or 2 halfwords at once){S, Q, SH, U, UQ, UH} × {ADD8, SUB8, ADD16, SUB16, ASX, SAX}: S and U set GE[3:0], Q and UQ saturate, SH and UH halve the result; SEL picks each byte by GE__SADD8 __UQSUB8 __SHADD16 __SASX __SEL ... (the same names with __)


Sum of absolute differencesUSAD8 USADA8__USAD8 __USADA8


16-bit multipliesSMULxy SMLAxy SMULWy SMLAWy SMLALxy (x, y = B bottom or T top half)__SMULBB __SMULBT __SMULTB __SMULTT


Dual 16-bit multipliesSMUAD SMUSD SMLAD SMLSD SMLALD SMLSLD (X: swap the halves of the second operand)__SMUAD __SMUADX __SMUSD __SMUSDX __SMLAD __SMLADX __SMLSD __SMLSDX; 64-bit accumulate: unsigned long long __SMLALD(x, y, acc), __SMLALDX __SMLSLD __SMLSLDX


Most significant wordSMMUL SMMLA SMMLS (R: rounded)__SMMUL __SMMLA


Pack and extendPKHBT PKHTB (with LSL #n / ASR #n), SXTB16 UXTB16 SXTAB SXTAH SXTAB16 UXTAB UXTAH UXTAB16 (optional ROR #8/16/24)__PKHBT(a, b, n) __PKHTB(a, b, n) __SXTB16 __UXTB16 __SXTAB16 __UXTAB16


ARMv8-MLDA LDAB LDAH STL STLB STLH, LDAEX LDAEXB LDAEXH STLEX STLEXB STLEXH (with no caches or second bus master they act like LDR/STR, LDREX/STREX), TT TTT (11.4), MRS/MSR MSPLIM PSPLIM, MSR APSR_g APSR_nzcvqg__get_MSPLIM __set_MSPLIM __get_PSPLIM __set_PSPLIM __get_APSR




The 64-bit accumulating instructions (SMLALD, SMLALxy ...) have no C intrinsic here. The intrinsics return unsigned for the SIMD forms and int otherwise, as CMSIS does; on the Cortex-M3 they are compile errors ("__SADD16() needs a core with the DSP extension"). The results were checked against values worked out by hand from Arm's instruction descriptions, not against a real M33.


/* m33dot/main.c - a dot product of 16-bit values, two at a time */
#pragma core "cortex-m33"
short x[4] = { 1, 2, 3, 4 };
short y[4] = { 5, 6, 7, 8 };
void main(void)
{
  unsigned *px = (unsigned *)x, *py = (unsigned *)y;
  int s = __SMLAD(px[0], py[0], 0);     /* 1*5 + 2*6 */
  int d = __SMLAD(px[1], py[1], s);     /* + 3*7 + 4*8 */
  char buf[4];
  buf[0] = '0' + d / 10; buf[1] = '0' + d % 10; buf[2] = 0;
  uart_puts("dot ");
  uart_puts(buf);
  uart_putc('\n');
}


11.3 Stack limit registers


MSPLIM and PSPLIM hold the lowest address the main and the process stack may use (bits 2-0 are 0). An instruction that would set SP below the limit of the stack in use (PUSH, STMDB/STMFD with sp!, ADD/SUB/MOV to sp, LDR into sp) is stopped before SP changes and raises a UsageFault with SCB_CFSR bit 20 (STKOF); with the UsageFault handler off (SCB_SHCSR bit 18) it becomes a HardFault. An exception whose frame would go below the limit is not stacked: SP is set to the limit, STKOF is set and the UsageFault (or HardFault) handler runs instead (simplification: real hardware keeps the original exception pending as well). In handler mode the limit is MSPLIM. MSR MSP/MSR PSP are not checked here (not verified against the architecture). Both limits are 0 after reset.


The VxWorks kernel guards task stacks with PSPLIM on the Cortex-M33 (VX_NO_STACK_PROTECT).


11.4 The ARMv8-M MPU


The same addresses as the ARMv7-M MPU (5.11), with different contents:




RegisterAddressContents


MPU_TYPE, MPU_CTRL, MPU_RNR0xE000ED90-98as on the Cortex-M3 (8 regions; CTRL b0 ENABLE, b1 HFNMIENA, b2 PRIVDEFENA)


MPU_RBAR0xE000ED9Cb31-5 BASE (the first address, 32-byte aligned), b4-3 SH (stored), b2-1 AP, b0 XN. No VALID/REGION bits: MPU_RNR picks the region.


MPU_RLAR0xE000EDA0b31-5 LIMIT (the region ends at LIMIT + 31), b3-1 AttrIndx (stored), b0 EN


RBAR_A1..A3, RLAR_A1..A30xE000EDA4-B8aliases for regions RNR+1 ... RNR+3 (RNR with bits 1-0 cleared)


MPU_MAIR0, MPU_MAIR10xE000EDC0, C4memory attributes, stored only (no caches here)




AP: 00 privileged read/write, 01 read/write for all, 10 privileged read only, 11 read only for all. A region is any multiple of 32 bytes; there are no sub-regions. An address in two enabled regions always faults (on the ARMv7-M MPU the higher region wins). No region: privileged code uses the default map if PRIVDEFENA is set; unprivileged code faults. The Peripherals window shows the regions with base and limit and warns about overlaps.


TT rd, rn asks the MPU about the address in rn (TTT: as unprivileged code): bits 7-0 MREGION, bit 16 MRVALID (the address is in exactly one enabled region), bit 18 R (readable), bit 19 RW (read/write). The Security fields stay 0 until TrustZone comes (phase 2c).


11.5 Floating-point unit


The FPU of this Cortex-M33 is FPv5 single precision: 32 registers s0-s31 of 32 bits and the status and control register FPSCR. The Registers window shows them (as numbers; the hex value in the tooltip) with the rounding mode and the flags.




RegisterAddressContents


SCB_CPACR0xE000ED88bits 23-20: access to the FPU (CP10, CP11). 0 after reset: the FPU is off, and an FP instruction is a UsageFault with SCB_CFSR bit 19 (NOCP). 0xF = full access; 0x5 = privileged only.


FPSCR(VMRS/VMSR)b31-28 N Z C V of the last compare; b26 AHP (stored only), b25 DN (NaN results are the default NaN 0x7FC00000), b24 FZ (flush subnormal inputs and results to zero), b23-22 RMode (0 to nearest, 1 towards +∞, 2 towards -∞, 3 towards zero); sticky flags b7 IDC (input denormal flushed), b4 IXC (inexact), b3 UFC (underflow), b2 OFC (overflow), b1 DZC (divide by zero), b0 IOC (invalid operation). C: __get_FPSCR(), __set_FPSCR(x).


FPU_FPCCR0xE000EF34b31 ASPEN (1 after reset): an FP instruction sets CONTROL bit 2 (FPCA), and an exception taken while FPCA is set stacks S0-S15 and FPSCR too; b30 LSPEN is stored, but lazy stacking is not modelled (the registers are stacked at once: the same contents)


FPU_FPCAR, FPU_FPDSCR0xE000EF38, 3CFPCAR is stored only; FPDSCR holds the AHP, DN, FZ and RMode bits that FPSCR gets when a new FP context starts (the first FP instruction in a handler, or after FPCA was cleared)




Exceptions. With FPCA set, the frame has 26 words: r0-r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR, then S0-S15, FPSCR and a reserved word; EXC_RETURN then has bit 4 clear (0xFFFFFFE1, 0xFFFFFFE9, 0xFFFFFFED) and the return restores the FP registers and FPCA. A handler starts with FPCA = 0.




GroupInstructions (all .F32)


ArithmeticVADD VSUB VMUL VDIV VNMUL VSQRT VABS VNEG; VMLA VMLS VNMLA VNMLS (multiply, round, add, round); VFMA VFMS VFNMA VFNMS (fused: rounded once); VMAXNM VMINNM


CompareVCMP VCMPE (with sm or #0.0; VCMPE also flags quiet NaNs), then VMRS APSR_nzcv, FPSCR to branch on the result; VSELEQ VSELGE VSELGT VSELVS


Convert and roundVCVT.S32.F32 / .U32.F32 (towards zero), VCVTR (FPSCR mode), VCVTA VCVTN VCVTP VCVTM, VCVT.F32.S32 / .F32.U32; fixed point VCVT.S32.F32 sd, sd, #fbits and back; VCVTB / VCVTT .F16.F32 and .F32.F16 (half precision in the bottom or top half); VRINTA VRINTN VRINTP VRINTM VRINTZ VRINTR VRINTX


Move, load, storeVMOV (sd, sm; sn, rt; rt, sn; two singles ↔ two core registers; VMOV.F32 sd, #imm for the values ±n/16 × 2e, n 16-31, e -3...4), VLDR VSTR ([rn, #imm], word aligned), VPUSH VPOP, VLDM VSTM (IA, DB, optional !), VMRS VMSR (FPSCR, MVFR0-2)




The results are correctly rounded IEEE 754 single precision in all four rounding modes, with subnormals, infinities, NaN propagation (a signalling NaN becomes quiet and sets IOC) and the flags. They were checked against hand-worked IEEE values and, in round to nearest, bit for bit against the soft-float library of the Cortex-M3. Underflow is detected before rounding (as Arm's pseudocode does, from memory: not verified). Not modelled: AHP (half precision is always IEEE), lazy stacking, the timing (every FP instruction takes one cycle; a real VDIV or VSQRT takes 14).


The C compiler on the Cortex-M33 uses the FPU for float (arithmetic, compares, int ↔ float); a float value still travels in a core register and as a function argument or result, as with GCC's -mfloat-abi=softfp, so code built for either core mixes freely and the shell's C interpreter works the same. sqrtf() and fabsf() become single VSQRT.F32 / VABS.F32 instructions (same results as the library; a program that defines its own sqrtf or fabsf keeps its function). double stays in the soft-float library. It defines __ARM_FP (4), __VFP_FP__ and __ARM_FEATURE_FMA. Because the startup files have no SystemInit() (where CMSIS projects turn the FPU on), main() of a bare-metal program that uses float or double sets CPACR bits 23-20 first: this emulator's own choice.


VxWorks on the Cortex-M33 turns the FPU on, switches the automatic FP stacking off (FPCCR = 0) and saves S0-S31 and FPSCR of every task at each context switch (whether or not it was spawned with VX_FP_TASK), and around the interrupt handlers, so the context switch code is the same as on the Cortex-M3. This is this emulator's own way; real VxWorks keeps FP state only for VX_FP_TASK tasks. A signal handler that uses floating point can disturb a float expression its task was in the middle of.


/* fpu/main.c - the rounding mode of the FPU */
#pragma core "cortex-m33"
float one = 1.0, three = 3.0;
unsigned bits(float f) { return *(unsigned *)&f; }
void hex(unsigned v)
{
  int i;
  for (i = 28; i >= 0; i -= 4)
    uart_putc("0123456789ABCDEF"[(v >> i) & 15]);
}
void main(void)
{
  uart_puts("RN ");
  hex(bits(one / three));            /* round to nearest: 0x3EAAAAAB */
  __set_FPSCR(3 << 22);              /* RMode = towards zero */
  uart_puts(" RZ ");
  hex(bits(one / three));            /* 0x3EAAAAAA */
  uart_putc('\n');
}


11.6 TrustZone (the Security Extension)


The CPU is either Secure (after reset) or Non-secure. Memory is Secure, Non-secure callable (NSC) or Non-secure, as the SAU says. There is no IDAU (the chip-defined attribution of real parts) and no address aliasing here: the board's one memory map is split by the SAU alone. With the SAU off everything is Secure (with ALLNS = 1: everything Non-secure). The system space 0xE0000000-0xEFFFFFFF belongs to whichever state accesses it.




RegisterAddressContents (Secure only: Non-secure code reads 0 and its writes are ignored)


SAU_CTRL0xE000EDD0b0 ENABLE, b1 ALLNS


SAU_TYPE, SAU_RNR0xE000EDD4, D88 regions; the region number for RBAR and RLAR


SAU_RBAR, SAU_RLAR0xE000EDDC, E0base (b31-5); limit (b31-5, the region ends at LIMIT + 31), b1 NSC, b0 enable. An address in no region, or in two, is Secure.


SCB_SFSR, SCB_SFAR0xE000EDE4, E8SecureFault cause: b0 INVEP (Non-secure code entered Secure code other than at an SG in NSC memory), b1 INVIS (bad integrity signature), b2 INVER (bad exception return), b3 AUVIOL (a Non-secure access to Secure memory), b4 INVTRAN (Secure code ran into Non-secure memory), b6 SFARVALID; write 1 to clear. SFAR: the address.


SCB_VTOR0xE000ED08the vector table of the current state (banked; VTOR_S starts at 0x08000000)


Non-secure copies0xE002E000-0xE002EFFFSecure code reaches the Non-secure bank of the SCB, MPU and SysTick registers here (for example SCB_VTOR_NS at 0xE002ED08)


SCB_AIRCR0xE000ED0Cb13 BFHFNMINS (HardFault, BusFault and NMI go to the Non-secure state), b14 PRIS (stored), b3 SYSRESETREQS


SCB_ICSR0xE000ED04b24 STTNS: the SysTick (there is one) belongs to the Non-secure state; PENDSVSET pends the PendSV of the state that writes it


SCB_SHCSR0xE000ED24b19 SECUREFAULTENA (otherwise a SecureFault becomes a HardFault), b4 SecureFault active


NVIC_ITNS0x40015018bit n = 1: IRQ n goes to the Non-secure state (on this board's NVIC; the address is this emulator's own, a real M33 has ITNS at 0xE000E380)




Banked registers (one copy per state; instructions use the current state's copy): MSP, PSP, MSPLIM, PSPLIM, CONTROL (nPRIV, SPSEL), PRIMASK, BASEPRI, VTOR, the MPU and the PendSV request. Secure code reads and writes the Non-secure copies with MRS/MSR MSP_NS, PSP_NS, MSPLIM_NS, PSPLIM_NS, CONTROL_NS, PRIMASK_NS, BASEPRI_NS, SP_NS (C: __TZ_get_MSP_NS(), __TZ_set_MSP_NS(x) ...). Own simplifications: SHPR, the SHCSR enables, CCR and CFSR are shared; PRIMASK or BASEPRI of either state masks all interrupts; FAULTMASK is not modelled.


Changing state. Non-secure code enters Secure code only by branching to an SG instruction in NSC memory (SG clears bit 0 of lr). Secure code returns with BXNS lr (bit 0 of the address = 0: Non-secure). Secure code calls Non-secure code with BLXNS rn: the return address and IPSR go on the Secure stack and lr becomes FNC_RETURN (0xFEFFFFFF); the Non-secure function returns with BX lr. Code addresses in this emulator have no Thumb bit, so bit 0 is 0 unless a program sets it.


Exceptions. Each exception is taken in its own state, with that state's vector table: SecureFault always Secure; HardFault, BusFault and NMI Secure unless BFHFNMINS; MemManage, UsageFault and SVC in the state that caused them; SysTick by STTNS; IRQs by ITNS. EXC_RETURN has b6 S (the interrupted code was Secure), b5 DCRS, b4 FType, b3 Mode, b2 SPSEL and b0 ES (the exception is Secure); for example 0xFFFFFFB8 for a Non-secure exception from Non-secure thread code on MSP. A Non-secure exception taken from Secure code also stacks the additional state context on the Secure stack (the integrity signature 0xFEFA125B, or 0xFEFA125A with an FP frame, a reserved word and r4-r11) and clears r0-r12 and the flags; the return checks the signature (INVIS) and restores them. Own simplification: for a Non-secure exception from Non-secure code no registers are cleared.


Instructions: SG, BXNS, BLXNS; TT, TTT, TTA, TTAT (from Secure code the result also has SREGION b15-8, SRVALID b17, NSR b20, NSRW b21 and S b22; IREGION and IRVALID stay 0: no IDAU).


C (as Arm's CMSE specification describes, with this emulator's limits):




FeatureWhat the compiler does


__attribute__((cmse_nonsecure_entry))the function body is labelled __acle_se_name and returns with BXNS after clearing r1-r3, r12 and the flags; name labels its veneer (SG then B __acle_se_name). All veneers sit together between the labels __sg_start and __sg_end, which the Secure start-up makes an NSC region. Secure code may not call an entry function itself: it would return to the Non-secure state. Arguments and the result must fit in registers.


typedef void __attribute__((cmse_nonsecure_call)) nsfunc_t(void);a call through a nsfunc_t * keeps r4-r11 on the Secure stack, clears them and the flags and uses BLXNS (at most 4 argument words). Only the typedef form is supported.


#include <arm_cmse.h>cmse_address_info_t, cmse_TT/TTT/TTA/TTAT, cmse_check_address_range (flags CMSE_MPU_READWRITE 1, CMSE_AU_NONSECURE 2, CMSE_MPU_UNPRIV 4, CMSE_MPU_READ 8, CMSE_MPU_NONSECURE 16, CMSE_NONSECURE 18), cmse_check_pointed_object, cmse_nsfptr_create (no change: the addresses have bit 0 = 0) and cmse_is_nsfptr.


cmse_nonsecure_caller()Inside a cmse_nonsecure_entry function: non-zero when the call came from the Non-secure state, 0 when Secure code called it through its veneer (a function pointer). It reads bit 0 of the return address that the entry function saved (SG from the Non-secure state clears it). Elsewhere it is an error (this emulator's own rule).


macros__ARM_FEATURE_CMSE is 3 in a Secure program and 1 in the Non-secure image




Not modelled: an IDAU and Secure/Non-secure address aliases, the second SysTick, FAULTMASK, lazy FP state preservation across the states and CMSE's clearing of the FP registers, the stack sealing of v8.1-M, and debug authentication (the debugger sees both states). The Map tab shows both images (the Non-secure one marked) and a main stack per state. Bit layouts were checked against Arm's CMSIS headers and the CMSE specification, and the behaviour against QEMU's Armv8-M model; nothing here was compared with real silicon.




12. The Cortex-M7 core


Choose it with the Board list, #pragma core "cortex-m7", or compatible = "arm,cortex-m7" in the cpu@0 node of a VxWorks board.dts (User Manual 8.1). Everything in chapters 1-10 applies, with the additions below. Programs written for the Cortex-M3 build and run unchanged (the M7 has the same ARMv7-M MPU). Try .


12.1 This emulator's Cortex-M7




ItemValue


ArchitectureARMv7E-M: Thumb-2 with the DSP extension (the instructions and intrinsics of 11.2) and the floating-point extension with double precision


SCB_CPUID0x411FC272 (Arm, part 0xC27; the revision r1p2 is this emulator's choice)


MPUARMv7-M (PMSAv7), 8 regions, as on the Cortex-M3 (5.11)


FPUFPv5 with double precision (FPv5-D16): D0-D15 over S0-S31 (12.2); MVFR0-2 read 0x10110221, 0x12000011, 0x00000040 (this emulator's reading of Arm's Cortex-M7 documentation, not verified)


Cachescontrol registers only (12.3): no cache is modelled


TCMITCM: 64 KB at 0x00000000, data only (12.4); the board RAM at 0x20000000 plays the DTCM


Not hereno stack limit registers, no TrustZone, no load-acquire/store-release (ARMv8-M only). The M7's options (FPU, cache and TCM sizes, MPU regions) are chosen when a chip is designed; the ones here are this emulator's own, not those of a particular NXP chip.


Timingas on the Cortex-M3: 1 instruction = 1 cycle. The M7's dual issue, its pipeline, branch prediction and the cost of cache misses are not modelled.




12.2 Double precision


Every single-precision instruction of 11.5 also has a .F64 form on D registers: VADD VSUB VMUL VDIV VNMUL VSQRT VABS VNEG VMLA VMLS VNMLA VNMLS VFMA VFMS VFNMA VFNMS VMAXNM VMINNM VSEL VRINT VCMP VCMPE. Conversions: VCVT.F64.F32 Dd, Sm and VCVT.F32.F64 Sd, Dm; VCVT{R,A,N,P,M}.S32.F64 Sd, Dm (also .U32) and VCVT.F64.S32 Dd, Sm. Moves and memory: VMOV Dd, Rt, Rt2 (Rt is the low word), VMOV Rt, Rt2, Dm, VMOV.F64 Dd, Dm, VMOV.F64 Dd, #imm, VLDR/VSTR Dd, [Rn, #imm] (the low word at the lower address), and D register lists in VPUSH VPOP VLDM VSTM ({d8-d15}). Fixed-point conversions of doubles (#fbits) are not modelled. Dn is S2n+1:S2n, so the exception frame, __fpu_save and the VxWorks context switch, which save S0-S31, keep the D registers too.


The results are computed exactly (with JavaScript big integers) and rounded once, in all four rounding modes, with subnormals, flush-to-zero, the default NaN and all the flags. They were checked bit for bit against JavaScript's IEEE doubles (round to nearest) and against the soft-float library of 4.11; the other modes against hand-worked values. Nothing was compared with real silicon.


The C compiler on the Cortex-M7 uses the FPU for double as well as float: arithmetic, compares, conversions to and from int, unsigned and float, ++/--, and sqrt()/fabs() (sqrtf()/fabsf() for float) become single instructions. A double still travels in r0:r1 and in memory (softfp, as float does on the M33), so the code mixes freely with code built for the other cores. Conversions between long long and double and the other maths functions stay in the library.


/* m7fpu/main.c - 1.0 / 3.0 with VDIV.F64 */
#pragma core "cortex-m7"
volatile double one = 1.0, three = 3.0;
void hex(unsigned v)
{
  int i;
  uart_puts("0x");
  for (i = 28; i >= 0; i -= 4)
    uart_putc("0123456789ABCDEF"[(v >> i) & 15]);
}
void main(void)
{
  double q = one / three;
  unsigned *w = (unsigned *)&q;
  hex(w[1]); uart_putc(' '); hex(w[0]); uart_putc('\n');
  while (1) { }
}


12.3 Cache control registers




RegisterAddressHere


SCB_CCR bits 16 DC, 17 IC, 18 BP0xE000ED14read/write: data cache, instruction cache, branch prediction on/off


SCB_CLIDR0xE000ED780x09000003: level 1 instruction and data caches


SCB_CTR0xE000ED7C0x8303C003: 32-byte lines


SCB_CCSIDR, SCB_CSSELR0xE000ED80, 0xE000ED84CSSELR bit 0 picks the cache; CCSIDR then reads 0xF00FE019 (data: 16 KB, 4 ways, 128 sets) or 0x201FE009 (instruction: 16 KB, 2 ways, 256 sets). The sizes are this emulator's own.


SCB_ICIALLU ICIMVAU DCIMVAC DCISW DCCMVAU DCCMVAC DCCSW DCCIMVAC DCCISW BPIALL0xE000EF50 - 0xE000EF78maintenance operations: accepted, and they do nothing (the Bus log shows them)




No cache is modelled, so memory is always coherent: a program that forgets to clean or invalidate the data cache around DMA works here but would fail on a real M7. The registers exist only on the Cortex-M7; on the other cores they are a bus fault.


12.4 Tightly coupled memory


The ITCM is 64 KB of RAM at 0x00000000 (0x00000000 - 0x0000FFFF). Programs and the debugger (Memory, Watch) can read and write it like RAM; code cannot run from it here, because this emulator runs code only from the flash. It is cleared at reset. The board's RAM at 0x20000000 is where a real M7 has its DTCM. On the other cores the addresses are a bus fault.


13. Two cores and the messaging unit


A program built with #pragma core1 (User Manual 8.3) runs on two cores. Core 0 is the core of the program that has the pragma, core 1 the core of the program it names; any two of the cores in chapters 11 and 12 (or the Cortex-M3) can be combined. TrustZone (#pragma nonsecure) and VxWorks (a device tree) are not available in a two-core program here.




ItemHere


Per coreregisters, flags, the NVIC enable, pending and priority bits, SysTick, the SCB (VTOR, SHCSR, CCR, fault status), the MPU, the FPU, the TrustZone bank, the exception state, the ITCM (Cortex-M7), its cycle count


Sharedflash, RAM, every board peripheral, the UART terminal, the MU; a peripheral's interrupt line reaches both NVICs


Startboth cores start at reset. Core 1 takes SP and PC from its own vector table at its FLASH origin (its VTOR points there)


Timingboth run at 1 MHz: after each instruction of the chosen core the other core runs until its cycle count catches up (round robin). Memory accesses are not arbitrated: two cores never collide here


Resetthe Reset button, a watchdog timeout and AIRCR SYSRESETREQ (from either core) reset both cores and the board (this emulator's simplification: a real i.MX resets a single core with its own reset controller)




13.1 Messaging unit (MU), 0x40019000


Both cores see the MU at the same address: core 0 uses side A, core 1 side B. The layout is this emulator's own, simpler than NXP's MU (which has the same idea: transmit and receive registers, status flags, general-purpose interrupts). Without a second core the addresses are a bus fault.




RegisterOffsetAccessMeaning


MU_TR0-MU_TR30x00-0x0Cwritesend a word: it appears in the other side's RRn, sets its RFn and clears my TEn


MU_RR0-MU_RR30x10-0x1Creadthe word the other side sent; reading clears my RFn and sets the other side's TEn


MU_SR0x20read / write 1 to clearbits 0-3 RFn (RRn is full), 4-7 TEn (my TRn has been read; 1 after reset), 8-11 GIPn (general interrupt n pending: write 1 to clear)


MU_CR0x24read/writebits 0-3 RIEn (interrupt while RFn), 4-7 TIEn (interrupt while TEn), 8-11 GIEn (interrupt while GIPn); writing 1 to bit 16+n raises general interrupt n on the other side (these bits read 0)




The MU is IRQ 7 (vector 23) on each core: pending while any enabled condition of that core's side holds. NVIC_EN bit 7 enables it; the two startup files of amp/ have the MU_IRQHandler entry. The Bus log shows every word sent and every general interrupt.


14. The Cortex-A55 core (AArch64)


Choose it with the Board list or #pragma core "cortex-a55" in an assembly file (User Manual 8.1). The Cortex-A55 is an application processor (ARMv8.2-A): it runs the 64-bit A64 instruction set, not Thumb-2: write A64 assembly, or C, which the compiler turns into A64 code (14.6). The board, its peripherals and the memory map stay the same: code in the flash at 0x08000000 (A64 instructions are 4 bytes, one per code slot), 64 KB RAM at 0x20000000. Try  (assembly) and  (C).


14.1 This emulator's Cortex-A55




ItemValue


Registersx0-x30 (64 bits; w0-w30 are their low 32 bits, and writing a w register clears the upper half), xzr/wzr (reads 0), sp = SP_EL0 or SP_EL1, PC; PSTATE: NZCV, DAIF (Debug, SError, IRQ, FIQ masks), SPSel, the exception level


MIDR_EL1, MPIDR_EL10x412FD050 (Arm, part 0xD05; r2p0 is this emulator's choice), 0x80000000 (core 0)


Exception levelsEL1 (kernel) and EL0 (applications). The core starts at EL1 with SP_EL1 = 0x20010000 (top of RAM), DAIF all masked, VBAR_EL1 = 0. EL2, EL3 and AArch32 are not modelled (HVC and SMC are undefined instructions).


Memorythe MMU (14.7) is off after reset: every address is physical, and data accesses are Device memory, so an unaligned load or store is an alignment fault (as on a real A55 with the MMU off). The FP/SIMD registers and caches are not modelled.


Timing1 instruction = 1 cycle at 1 MHz; the A55's pipeline is not modelled
